text:
Marguerite found the book where she always did on Thursdays: wedged between the flour bins and the cooling racks, as if it had climbed in through the wall. *A Field Guide to Coastal Birds*, spine cracked, a faded library stamp inside the cover. Due date long past.

Eleven Thursdays now. She'd asked the day staff, checked the locks, even stayed late once with a thermos and a rolling pin. Nothing. The book simply appeared between two and four a.m., and she never caught the moment.

Tonight it was heavier. She opened it and a folded square of receipt paper slid out.

*I keep meaning to bring it back to the library, but I walk past your window on the way and the light is on, and I think: somebody is awake. Then I leave it here instead. Sorry. I'll stop if you ask me to.*

Marguerite read it twice. Behind her the ovens ticked, and the first trays of rye waited under their cloths.

She turned the receipt over, found a pencil stub behind her ear, and wrote on the back: *Don't stop.* Then she tucked it inside the cover, set the book on the sill by the front window, and left the light on.

Thursdays at 3 a.m., Dov finds the book on the flour bin. Always the same one: *A Field Guide to Coastal Birds*, spine cracked, stamped DUE in a purple that's been dead since the nineties.

He's never caught anyone. The back door sticks, so whoever it is must have a key, or a very good shoulder.

Tonight he's elbow-deep in rye when he spots it, and the book's a little fatter than usual. A note, folded small, poking out near the sandpiper plates.

He wipes his hands on his apron. Not well. Leaves a floury thumbprint right across the paper, which feels rude, but there it is.

*Your sourdough smells like my mother's street. I can't come in. I'm not ready to. But I thought the birds should live somewhere warm.*

Dov reads it twice. Then a third time, mostly to the part about the street.

Honestly? He's not a sentimental guy. He once threw out a perfectly good wedding cake over a typo. But he stands there with the oven ticking behind him, and the loaves going past their proof, and he doesn't care.

He pulls a pencil from behind his ear, flips the note over, and writes: *Back door's open at 4. Bread's free.*

Then he props the door with a brick.

The book drop was a milk crate by the back door, and every Thursday around two, Imre found something in it that wasn't milk. First week: *A Field Guide to Mushrooms of the Northeast*, Carver Street Library stamp on the flyleaf, due date long past. Second week, the same book. Third week, the same.

He'd stopped reshelving it in his head. It lived on the flour bench now, between the scale and the tub of rye starter, its cover gone soft with dough-dusted thumbprints.

Tonight he slid the crate out with his hip, hands still in oven mitts, and the book was there again, heavier than usual. A yellow square of paper stuck out near page 112.

He peeled off the mitts. The note was in pencil, small, slanted hard to the right.

*Your door smells better than the library. I keep meaning to bring it to the right place. Is the morel on this page the one you use? —T.*

Imre looked at the page. Someone had circled nothing; the morel sat there, wrinkled and brown.

He pulled the pencil from behind his ear, flipped the note over, and wrote *No. Never used one.* Then, after a moment, he added *Come at five, there's bread.* He pressed it back into the book.

Marguerite found the book on the steel table by the back door, under the bench where the bread peels hang. *A Field Guide to Coastal Birds*. The Harbor Street branch stamp inside the cover gave a due date in March. The mail slot in that door had been nailed shut years ago, but the delivery hatch beside it, the one the flour man used, never latched properly.

Eleven Thursdays. She had asked the day staff and checked the hatch for scratches, and once she stayed past four with her coat on. Nothing. The book turned up between two and four, and she was always at the ovens, her back to the door, when it did.

Tonight a grocery receipt from Pell's was folded into the page on oystercatchers. The ink had gone blotchy where someone pressed too hard.

*I keep meaning to take this back to the library. Then I pass your door and there's the smell of bread and I put it down instead. I can stop if you want.*

She smelled of salt, she thought, whoever it was, because the pages did.

Marguerite pulled a pencil from her apron and wrote on the back of the receipt: *Bring it Thursday. I'll have a roll.* She tucked it in at the oystercatchers, set the book on the hatch ledge, and put a warm roll in a paper bag beside it.
